newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Kaunda campaigns for Zambia poll boycott.
newsitem.headline: Kaunda campaigns for Zambia poll boycott.

text.p: Zambian opposition leader Kenneth Kaunda called on Saturday for a mass boycott of elections next Monday, saying it would nullify the result and open the way for new, fairer polls.
"There is a deep-rooted crisis in this country," the former president told an anti-election rally in a dusty, dirt-poor township outside the capital, Lusaka.
"If you are hungry because of what this government has done to you, please don't vote on Monday. Go to tend the garden at dawn and don't come back till night."

President Frederick Chiluba, who ended 27 years of one-party rule by Kaunda in 1991, looks certain to win a second five-year term because Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP) led six smaller parties in a boycott of the presidential and parliamentary polls.

The boycott came after Chiluba supporters changed the law to ban presidential candidates whose parents were born abroad -- with Kaunda, of Malawian parents, the obvious target. Foreign aid donors froze help with Zambia's heavy debt servicing in protest.
Chiluba held a "grand finale" campaign rally in Lusaka, reminding Zambians of secret police control under Kaunda's rule, which left the country economically devastated.

Although Kaunda cannot run, he has been the focus of attacks by Chiluba's Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD). Chiluba's four remaining rivals pose no threat, but political analysts say the MMD may lose some support over it anti-Kaunda manoeuvres.

Chiluba, hailed in 1991 as a breath of democracy and peaceful change in Africa, rejected South African President Nelson Mandela's appeal on Thursday to postpone the vote pending efforts to persuade Kaunda's UNIP to participate.
Kaunda's Zambia hosted the headquarters of Mandela's anti-apartheid African National Congress and its armed wing during 30 years in exile, which ended in 1990.
Chiluba tried on Saturday to mend fences with South Africa, which had been angered by Zambian ministers telling Mandela to mind his own business.

"Mr Mandela never interfered at any time. Mr Mandela has a tremendous attachment to this country. He has been instrumental in asking for dialogue between Mr Kaunda and myself to ensure peace," Chiluba told reporters, adding he had banned ministers from making more comments on the issue.

However, Kaunda thanked donor countries and Mandela for their support, pressing ahead on Saturday with his campaign to get people to hand him their voting cards as a sign of their intention to join the boycott.
A flawed voter registration system has seen only a quarter of the 4.6 million eligible voters given voting cards.

Although diplomats saw little chance for the man who led Zambia to independence from Britain in 1964, Kaunda said once results were known on Wednesday he would call on the chief justice to take over as acting president, form an interim government and call fresh elections.
